sn10.5:1.1: The commentary explains that Sānu was a disillusioned novice who had returned home planning to disrobe. | Sānu was perhaps named after the planet Saturn (Sanskrit _śani_; cf. [sn10.7]()). The Sanskrit word for planet (_graha_, cf. Pali _gayha_ at [dn20:17.3]()) shows their role as “seizers”. The later Suśrutasaṁhitā-uttaratantra details the entities that cause such seizures in children (60), corresponding to the nine planets (27). Seizures or fits were treated as medical, spiritual, and astrological in cause and remedy.
sn10.5:1.2: Elsewhere we find possession by Māra expressed as _anvāviṭṭha_, literally “inhabited”, where the victims are made to behave badly but are otherwise normal ([sn4.18:1.4](), [mn50:14.2](); cf. Sanskrit _āviṣṭa_). _Gahita_ here is also used for Rāhu “seizing” the Sun and Moon ([sn2.10:1.2]()). The commentary says he was shaking on the ground, eyes rolling and mouth foaming, i.e. having a “seizure”. This was not ill-motivated, for the _yakkha_ was trying to prevent him from disrobing. Compare those who, though “seized by a gandharva” (_gandharvagṛhīta_), remain perfectly cogent (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.1, 3.7.1).
sn10.5:1.3: PTS editions insert an extra verse below, but it seems to be a scribal error.
sn10.5:2.1: See [an3.70]() for a detailed description of the eight-factored sabbath.
sn10.5:6.2: It’s interesting that the Buddha cites a _yakkha_ saying to someone recovering from a _yakkha_-induced seizure. At [thig12.1:12.1]() these lines are attributed to the nun Puṇṇikā.
sn10.5:8.1: Sānu has recovered from his seizure to see his weeping mother. This verse appears without any context at [thag1.44]().
sn10.5:9.1: Here’s the plot twist: the mother’s real worry is not the seizure, but that her son will fall prey to desire and suffering. See [sn20.10:3.5](), “For it is death in the training of the Noble One to reject the training and return to a lesser life.”
sn10.5:10.3: This is, I think, the only case in the EBTs where “inferno” might be suggested for _naraka_. Elsewhere in early Pali, however, it means “cliff, abyss” ([mn49:5.9](), mn86:6.15](), [snp3.11:28.4](), [thag16.8:4.2]()).
sn10.5:11.1: Here we see the origin of the term of address _bhante_, i.e. “good luck to thee”.
